cross_module_architecture.dimension_character: Structurally this is a clean codebase for its size: no import cycles at all, a strictly one-way types/lib/hooks/components/App layering that a newcomer could redraw from memory, no import-time side effects, and the two genuinely cross-cutting singletons both exposed through the same subscribe-plus-hook protocol with the reasoning written down beside them. The one seam that could have gone wrong - a Node MCP package reaching into a browser app's source tree - is documented in the README, justified in the code, and routed through a deliberately dependency-free protocol module. What pulls it down is a missing shared boundary rather than a violated one: the four non-character card types have no owning module, so their save/export workflow is copied into four editors plus a fifth character variant, and the app/MCP seam is held together by a duplicated type and a stale tsconfig include list.
cross_module_architecture.score_rationale: The dimension anchors for 80 describe recurring boundary violations, coupling hotspots, and hub modules that make changes ripple unexpectedly - none of that is present here, and the verified zero-cycle, one-way graph is stronger than most codebases this size. It falls short of 90-plus because a developer changing how a card is saved or exported edits five near-identical call sites, and because the cross-package contract is asserted in prose and casts rather than enforced by the compiler. 86.5 reflects coherent, intentional boundaries with one genuinely missing abstraction and two small honesty gaps at the package seam.

high_level_elegance.dimension_character: The skeleton is genuinely good: layers point one way, each src/lib subdirectory owns one capability and opens with a comment explaining why it exists, and the MCP server's boundary with the app is stated and honoured. What a new engineer would struggle to explain is the app's central domain concept — the five card types — which has no owner: the character card is owned by the shell while the other four editors are self-contained copies of one another, and the type union that names them is redeclared in five places and cast across. So the quality is uneven by area rather than uniformly weak: the plumbing is exemplary, the card-type domain is a copy-paste family with a missing abstraction.
high_level_elegance.score_rationale: Strong layer discipline, honest module docs, a README that matches runtime reality, and clean single-owner registries (PLATFORMS, NAV_SECTIONS) push this above the 'solid but uneven' anchor. Pulling it down is recurring, structural friction rather than nits — the four-way replicated non-character editor with no owning module, the asymmetric ownership between character and non-character cards, five parallel declarations of the card-type union with `as CardType` casts, and two sources of truth for the blank card while one of them claims to be the only one. That is exactly the 80-anchor experience: mostly well-served, with repeated 'why is this one different?' moments in the app's most central domain.

convention_outlier.dimension_character: Surface conventions in this codebase are unusually tight: a developer who reads one component, one lib module or one editor can predict the shape of every sibling — default-export function plus a local Props interface, named exports and camelCase in lib/, a shared editor scaffold, colocated tests, `cb_`-prefixed storage keys, and semantic Tailwind tokens. The drift that exists is behavioral rather than cosmetic, and it clusters where the code was extended one card type at a time: DecodePNG never adopted the cardShape classifier its sibling ImportPNG uses (and copies CHARACTER_KEYS instead of importing it), App.tsx preserves library identity for characters but drops it for the other four types on the same bridge path, and useUnsavedWarning guards only character state. Those, plus the inline-hex CodeEditor island and four parallel names for one card-kind union, are the moments where a learned pattern stops holding.
convention_outlier.score_rationale: The consistency is systemic and the outliers are countable and local, which keeps this well above the 80 anchor's 'recurring friction' — but the outliers are not cosmetic: three of them are protocol divergences with real consequences (mislabelled cards mis-loaded, agent-opened cards duplicated on save, unsaved work lost silently in four editors), which is more than the 90 anchor's 'isolated rough edges'. Scored just above 80 because a developer can trust the visible conventions almost everywhere yet cannot assume that a shared helper adopted by one sibling was adopted by the rest.

error_consistency.dimension_character: Error handling here is designed rather than accumulated: the bridge, the PNG decoder and the LLM sorter each have an explicit failure vocabulary, every swallowed error carries a written justification, and nothing anywhere logs-and-continues. The friction is concentrated in the React layer, where the same IndexedDB and file-read calls are guarded in five editors and completely unguarded in Library.tsx and the two image drop paths, and where the save-to-library catch throws away messages the export path right above it reports verbatim. A developer would trust the library and protocol layers immediately but would have to check each component individually to know whether a failure reaches the user at all.
error_consistency.score_rationale: The systemic strengths are real and unusual — actionable user-facing messages, a single conversion point per protocol boundary, corrupt-vs-absent distinguished in the decoder, and zero silent console swallows — which puts this above the 80 'solid but uneven' anchor. abstraction_fitness.dimension_character: Over-abstraction is essentially absent here: there are no barrels, no single-implementation interface ecosystems, no delegation chains, and the one generic in the codebase is genuinely polymorphic — platform behaviour is a data table read by two switch dispatchers, and the MCP server reuses the app's own modules rather than a parallel copy. What a developer actually hits is the opposite failure: one card-editor shape is written out four times (four editors, four App state clusters, two five-callback prop bags) and the LibraryCard type models a tagged union by hand, so seventeen `as LoreBook`-style assertions do the narrowing TypeScript would have done for free. The strengths are systemic across lib/ and mcp/, and the weakness is a single well-delimited cluster in the non-character card editing path — but that cluster is where most feature work lands.
abstraction_fitness.score_rationale: Pushing the score up: every layer that exists pays for itself, the wire protocol is shared rather than duplicated across the two processes, and the platform matrix is data instead of a class hierarchy — a developer navigating lib/ never fights indirection. Pulling it down: adding a sixth card type today means identical edits in six files, and the hand-rolled LibraryCard union forces unchecked casts at every consumption site, which is a type layer that adds ceremony without adding safety. That is recurring, predictable friction confined to one subsystem, which places this between the 80 anchor's 'solid but uneven' and the 90 anchor's 'isolated rough edges'.

low_level_elegance.dimension_character: Function internals are, on the whole, unusually disciplined for an app of this size: guard clauses first, small named predicates instead of inline regex thickets, explicit functional state updaters, bounded loops with stated limits, and comments that record why a shape was chosen rather than restating the code. api_surface_coherence.dimension_character: The seams that matter most here — the bridge wire protocol, its RPC handlers, and the MCP tool set — are genuinely coherent: named param/result types, one shape per call, an observable-singleton pattern reproduced identically in three unrelated modules, and converter/download/editor-prop families that a developer can predict from one example. authorization_consistency.dimension_character: This is a local-first app with a single real authorization boundary — the MCP bridge — and that boundary is unusually well built: mutual challenge-response over a shared token with server-proves-first ordering, constant-time comparison on both halves, origin allowlisting, loopback bind, single-session enforcement, handshake timeouts, and a README that explicitly retracts its own earlier weaker claim. Both are limited and fixable within one module rather than systemic drift, so this sits near the boundary between 'strong' and 'mostly consistent with limited exceptions'.

The friction is concentrated in two places a developer meets constantly — a 29-file flat src/components/ that mixes routed pages, single-parent feature children and shared primitives with no folder or naming signal separating them, and an unmarked browser/node boundary where a separate npm package (mcp/) reaches back through ../../src/lib into four modules that look identical to their browser-only siblings. Quality is therefore uneven rather than broadly weak: the layout tells you where domains live but not what owns a component or which shared code has a second consumer.
package_organization.score_rationale: The clean acyclic layering, cohesive lib/ domain folders and co-located tests are systemic strengths that keep this above the 70 'can't trust patterns' band. What holds it under 90 is real navigational drag rather than aesthetics: src/components/ is exactly the 'flat directory mixing unrelated concerns' case the 80-anchor describes, and the mcp/ cross-package reach has already produced measurable drift (mcp/tsconfig.json's include list is missing two of the four modules it imports). Scoring at the solid-but-uneven anchor because a developer would navigate lib/ confidently and search components/ every time.

initialization_coupling.dimension_character: Import-time behaviour here is disciplined to an unusual degree: no environment reads anywhere, no storage or network touched at module scope, IndexedDB and the multi-gigabyte WebLLM engine both behind lazy getters with dynamic imports, zero import cycles across 63 files, and shared lib modules that are genuinely isomorphic so the Node MCP server imports them unshimmed. Where module-level mutable state does exist — bridge state, engine state, sorter settings — it is deliberate, documented, and exposed through getState/subscribe pairs consumed via useSyncExternalStore, which is the right contract rather than an ambient global. The one soft spot is concentrated in src/lib/bridge/client.ts, where the host-registration and connect steps form an implicit ordering contract that nothing enforces and whose violation would fail silently through optional chaining.
initialization_coupling.score_rationale: The strengths are systemic and verifiable rather than incidental — a developer can import essentially any module in this tree without triggering side effects or worrying about sequence, which is what the 90 anchor describes. It falls short of that because the bridge client concentrates several implicit-ordering hazards in one place (nullable `host` guarded only by statement order, silent optional-chained no-op on violation, initBridge bypassing the manualDisconnect latch, no effect cleanup) and the sorter-settings store's subscribe-vs-sample asymmetry holds only while there is a single writer. These are latent rather than active, so they read as isolated rough edges, not recurring friction — hence a score near the strong band rather than in the uneven-80s.

design_coherence.dimension_character: The lib layer is genuinely well designed: functions are focused, the biggest file earns its size through a single coherent responsibility, and behaviour that varies by card type or platform is expressed as data tables rather than branches. The component layer tells a different story — the same five-card-type axis that lib handles with tables is handled in components by copy-paste, producing four near-identical editor shells and five hand-written per-type branch chains, so quality on this dimension is consistent within a layer but uneven across the codebase. A developer reading any one file is well served; a developer adding a sixth card type has to touch roughly ten files and replicate the same shape in each.
design_coherence.score_rationale: The strengths are systemic in src/lib — data-driven vocabulary and field tables, no wrapper chains, no single-implementation interfaces, no injected-for-testability ceremony — which argues for the upper 80s. What pulls it down is one broad, repeated structural pattern rather than scattered noise: ~130 lines of logic and JSX duplicated four times across the card editors, the four-callback fanout restated at five call sites, and a blank-card constant defined twice. That is exactly the 80 anchor's 'repeated patterns that should be data-driven', and the breadth of it (four editor files plus five fanout sites) places the score just under it.

contract_coherence.dimension_character: Inside any single library module the contracts are unusually trustworthy: nullable strategy functions declare their nulls, JSDoc explains not just what a function does but which past bug its contract now prevents, and getters are genuinely pure. The failures cluster at exactly two seams — the app/MCP bridge boundary and the `unknown` rawData union — where types are asserted rather than honoured, so an MCP-declared tool contract ('only the fields you pass are touched', a script card's `code` field) does not survive the round trip into the app's own types. A developer would trust what they read within src/lib, then be surprised the first time an agent-created card opens blank or a bridge update silently drops the stored PNG.
contract_coherence.score_rationale: Strong intra-module discipline and a very small escape-hatch census push this above the 70 line: patterns learned in one lib module do hold in the next. What pulls it down to the mid-70s is that the seam defects are not cosmetic — update_card's documented no-touch guarantee is contradicted by pngData/platform loss, create_script's schema names a field the consuming type does not have, and validateTavernCardV2's signature is so far from its real accepted input that every caller including its own tests casts past it. That is 'solid but uneven' with two genuinely surprising APIs rather than the isolated local mismatches an 85+ would imply.

logic_clarity.dimension_character: Control flow here is unusually disciplined at the syntactic level: guard clauses and early returns dominate, switches are exhaustive over discriminated unions, timer hooks clear before re-arming, and almost every non-obvious branch carries a comment naming the concrete failure it prevents rather than restating the code. The weakness is not redundant branching but claims the logic does not keep — a handshake whose HMAC has no domain separation and so does not actually gate on the token, a lorebook normaliser that three of four entry paths bypass while a sibling line proves the un-normalised shape arrives, a filename effect that four editors ship without the guard App.tsx documents, and two doc comments that state bounds the code does not enforce. So a developer reading a single function will almost always find it honest and traceable; a developer following a value across module seams will occasionally find the stated invariant is not the enforced one.
logic_clarity.score_rationale: The mechanical targets of this dimension are essentially absent — no identical branches, no dead paths after return, no always-true conditions, no boolean-returning if/else — and the detector's own async/stub hits proved to be false positives on inspection, which argues for the 90 band. What pulls it back toward 80 is that this dimension is about logic that provably does what it claims, and four separate places fail that test, one of them defeating the bridge's authentication entirely and one repeating across four sibling editors where the correct guard already exists in App.tsx. Isolated correctness bugs behind otherwise clear code, plus one repeated cluster, place this at solid-with-recurring-friction rather than strong.

type_safety.dimension_character: The baseline discipline here is genuinely strong: strict mode on both packages, a clean tsc run, essentially no `any`, no escape-hatch comments, no non-null assertions, and the truly untrusted edges (foreign platform JSON, LLM output, MCP tool input) are validated field-by-field at runtime instead of being asserted into shape. The weakness is concentrated on exactly one axis — card-type polymorphism. The same five-value union is redeclared six times, LibraryCard encodes its variant invariant in comments rather than as a discriminated union, and the PNG decoder deliberately widens its key back to `string`, so the import/library/bridge path carries roughly fifteen load-bearing assertions the compiler cannot check.

issues.summary: Security-critical HMAC handshake in bridge/protocol.ts is pure and node-testable but has zero tests
issues.suggestion: Add src/lib/bridge/protocol.test.ts asserting: proveToken is deterministic for a given (token, message) and differs when either changes; the hex output is 64 lowercase chars; safeEqual is true for identical strings and false for equal-length one-bit differences, differing lengths, and the empty string; and that a wrong token fails the app-side verification.
evidence: protocol.ts implements the mutual challenge-response the file's own comment says exists because 'loopback is not an authentication boundary': proveToken() HMAC-SHA256 hex and safeEqual() constant-time compare.

safeEqual returns early on a length mismatch and otherwise XOR-accumulates; proveToken pads each byte to two hex digits. Both are exactly the kind of code where a silent regression weakens the check rather than breaking it visibly.
Both functions are pure and depend only on crypto.subtle and TextEncoder, available in the Node 18 runtime the suite already uses — no environment work needed. Neither appears in any test file.

evidence: mcp/package.json defines no test script and mcp/src contains no test files.

protocol.ts states 'This file is imported by both sides. Keep it dependency-free' and carries BRIDGE_PROTOCOL_VERSION, bumped 'when the shape below changes incompatibly' — but nothing verifies the two sides agree on frame shapes, version, or close codes.
A protocol change therefore surfaces only as a runtime handshake failure between two separately built packages.

issues.summary: detectPlatform is an ordered heuristic chain on the import path with no tests, unlike its tested sibling detectCardShape

issues.summary: src/components/ is 29 flat files mixing routed pages, single-parent children and shared primitives
issues.suggestion: Split by measured fan-in into three purpose-named folders, no new abstraction and no barrel files. Stage 1 (shared, lowest risk): create src/components/ui/ and git mv TagInput.tsx ResizableTextArea.tsx TextAreaField.tsx ImageDropzone.tsx ConfirmModal.tsx ConfirmClearPanel.tsx JSONView.tsx RawPreview.tsx into it. Stage 2: create src/components/pages/ and move the 13 App-mounted views (CreateCard, ImportPNG, DecodePNG, Templates, Settings, HelpAbout, Library, LoreBookEditor, ScriptEditor, ScenarioEditor, PersonaEditor, Sidebar, ErrorBoundary). Stage 3: leave the remaining single-parent children beside their parent page or under src/components/editor/ (CardPreviewPanel, CharacterEditor, PlatformSelector, FieldCompatibility, SmartImportPanel, SorterSettings, BridgeStatusLight, LlmStatusLight). After each stage run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build`; relative import paths are the only thing to fix and tsc lists every one.
evidence: 29 .tsx files, 5592 LOC, zero subdirectories; directory_profiles reports avg_fan_in 1.7 across them.

Measured fan-in splits them into three groups with different ownership: 13 files imported only by App.tsx (routed pages), 8 files with exactly one importer (CardPreviewPanel, CharacterEditor, JSONView, RawPreview <- CreateCard; PlatformSelector <- CardPreviewPanel; SorterSettings <- SmartImportPanel; BridgeStatusLight, LlmStatusLight <- Sidebar), and 6 files with fan-in 2-5 that are true shared primitives (TagInput 5, ResizableTextArea 5, ConfirmClearPanel 4, ImageDropzone 4, TextAreaField 3, ConfirmModal 2).

Nothing in the filename encodes which group a file is in: the 'Panel' suffix covers a 496-LOC feature child (CardPreviewPanel), a 432-LOC feature child (SmartImportPanel) and a 48-LOC shared primitive (ConfirmClearPanel).
Consequence: a developer editing CardPreviewPanel.tsx cannot tell from the tree that only CreateCard renders it, and editing ConfirmClearPanel.tsx gives no signal that four editors depend on it.

issues.summary: Bridge host must be registered before initBridge(), enforced only by statement order; wrong order fails silently

Every consumer optional-chains: `host?.onLibraryChanged?.()` and `host?.openCard(saved)` at lines 358, 359, 372, 373, 386. An `app.open` RPC arriving before registration therefore resolves successfully to the MCP server while doing nothing in the UI — the agent is told the card was opened when it was not.

issues.summary: initBridge() calls open() without honouring the manualDisconnect latch, so a re-entry can strand status at "connecting"

If initBridge runs while manualDisconnect is true, `open()` sets status "connecting" at line 140, then `onclose` hits `if (manualDisconnect) return;` at line 232 and never reports anything — the MCP light stays on "connecting" indefinitely with no error text.
Unreachable today only by accident: App.tsx's effect deps are all `useCallback(..., [])` so the effect runs once, but nothing in client.ts documents or defends that assumption.

issues.reasoning: 649 lines with one responsibility — turn a text blob into card fields. Its state — authed, serverNonce, handshakeTimer — is per-connection and genuinely belongs in the connection closure; hoisting it would require inventing a connection object to hold what the closure already holds. Nesting is inherent to the problem.

The branching is two backends (runWebLlm, runEndpoint) behind one entry point, each a single focused function, with schema, prompts and result shaping all derived from FIELD_DOCS/TARGET_FIELDS rather than restated per target. coerceJson and toParsedPersona are separate and small. issues.summary: The five card-type values are redeclared as six separate types plus three literal arrays, bridged by `as` casts
issues.suggestion: Keep one declaration. Export `const CARD_TYPES = ["character","lorebook","script","scenario","persona"] as const` and `type CardType = typeof CARD_TYPES[number]` from src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts (already shared by both packages), then re-export it as LibraryCardType/CardShape rather than redeclaring, derive ALLOWED_CARD_TYPES and the MCP z.enum from CARD_TYPES, replace NonCharType with Exclude<CardType, "character">, and import CHARACTER_KEYS in DecodePNG.tsx. The five `as CardType` casts in bridge/client.ts then delete themselves.
evidence: LibraryCardType (src/types/index.ts:163), CardShape (src/lib/cardShape.ts:13) and CardType (src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts:97) are byte-identical unions declared in three modules.

NonCharType (src/components/DecodePNG.tsx:13) is the same union minus "character"; ALLOWED_CARD_TYPES (src/lib/bridge/client.ts:350) and the z.enum at mcp/src/index.ts:81 restate the values again as data.
CHARACTER_KEYS is exported from src/lib/cardShape.ts:16 and independently re-declared at src/components/DecodePNG.tsx:11.
Because the unions are structurally equal but nominally separate, src/lib/bridge/client.ts uses `as CardType` at lines 281, 312, 360, 367 and 374 to move values between them; nothing checks these.

issues.summary: decodeCharaFromPng returns `key: string | null` although it only ever emits a MetadataKey, forcing casts in both consumers
issues.suggestion: Type the array as `const KNOWN_KEYS: readonly MetadataKey[] = [...]` (or derive both from a single const tuple) and change decodeCharaFromPng's return to `key: MetadataKey | null`. `key in NON_CHAR_META` then narrows on its own and the three `as NonCharType` casts in DecodePNG.tsx can go.
evidence: src/lib/pngMetadata/index.ts:128 holds `const knownKeys = ["chara", ...]` as an untyped string[] in a module that already imports MetadataKey (line 1) and uses it for the encode direction (line 192).

foundKey is only assigned inside `if (!foundJson && knownKeys.includes(keyword))` (line 162), so the return value is provably a MetadataKey, yet the signature at line 117 declares `key: string | null`.

Consumers pay for the lost narrowing: src/components/DecodePNG.tsx:80 and 190-194 write `result.key as NonCharType` even after guarding with `key in NON_CHAR_META`, and shapeForKey (src/lib/cardShape.ts:19) has to accept a bare string and re-test the literals.

issues.summary: bridge/client.ts bodyOf() is annotated Record<string, string> but returns objects holding arrays and nested records
issues.suggestion: Change bodyOf's return type to Record<string, unknown> | undefined — that is what the data actually is, it removes the `as unknown as` double cast and the compensating cast at line 365, and summarise()'s two reads only need a typeof check on character_version and version.
evidence: src/lib/bridge/client.ts:289-292: `function bodyOf(c: LibraryCard): Record<string, string> | undefined` reaches its value through `c.cardData?.data as unknown as Record<string, string>`.

The real type there is TavernCardV2Data, whose members include alternate_greetings: string[], tags: string[], character_book?: CharacterBook and extensions: Record<string, unknown> — none of which are strings.
The non-character branch is worse: `c.rawData as Record<string, string> | undefined` re-labels an `unknown` that holds arbitrary lorebook/script/scenario bodies.
The falsehood is not inert: updateCard (line 365) spreads bodyOf(existing) into the merge and then has to cast it back with `merged as Record<string, unknown>` to pass it on.

issues.summary: `parsed as LoreBook` on the PNG and library paths bypasses the only code that normalises SillyTavern's object-keyed entries
issues.suggestion: Export parseSillyTavernLorebook from a lib module (e.g. src/lib/loreBook.ts) and run every inbound lorebook through it: replace `parsed as LoreBook` in ImportPNG.tsx/DecodePNG.tsx and `card.rawData as LoreBook` in App.tsx/Library.tsx with parseSillyTavernLorebook(parsed). That makes the LoreBook annotation earned on all three routes instead of one.
evidence: parseSillyTavernLorebook (src/components/LoreBookEditor.tsx:50) exists precisely because ST entries can be an object keyed by numeric strings or a plain array, and it also fills in every missing field.
It is called from exactly one place — the drag-a-JSON-file handler at line 152.

The PNG import path asserts instead: src/components/ImportPNG.tsx:132 `onLoadLorebook?.(parsed as LoreBook, imageSrc)` on a value straight out of JSON.parse; src/components/DecodePNG.tsx:116 does the same; the library path does `card.rawData as LoreBook` at src/App.tsx:229 and src/components/Library.tsx:132.

LoreBookEditor then trusts the annotation immediately — line 97 reads `initialBook?.entries[0]?.id` and lines 128-142 call .find/.map on book.entries — so an object-shaped `entries` reaching the editor by PNG is a runtime failure the type system was told could not happen.

issues.summary: LibraryCard keeps its cardType/cardData/rawData invariant in comments, so ~10 call sites re-assert it by hand
issues.suggestion: Split LibraryCard into a discriminated union over cardType — { cardType: "character"; cardData: TavernCardV2 } | { cardType: "lorebook"; rawData: LoreBook } | ... sharing a LibraryCardBase for the common id/name/tags/timestamp fields. Narrowing on card.cardType then supplies the payload type at all eight App.tsx/Library.tsx sites and the casts disappear rather than being replaced by anything.
evidence: src/types/index.ts:184-186 documents the rule in trailing comments: `cardData?: TavernCardV2;   // present when cardType === "character"` and `rawData?: unknown;  // present when cardType is lorebook | script | scenario`.

Every consumer therefore switches on cardType and asserts the payload itself — src/App.tsx:229-238 (four `as` casts), src/components/Library.tsx:132-138 (four more), plus `card.rawData as { version?: string } | null` at Library.tsx:20 and the bodyOf branch at src/lib/bridge/client.ts:290-291.
src/lib/library/index.ts:88-90 also treats cardType as possibly absent (`c.cardType ?? "character"`) despite the field being declared required.

issues.summary: parseSillyTavernLorebook takes `any`, so its `const scan_depth: number = raw.scan_depth ?? 50` annotations are unchecked
issues.suggestion: Change the parameter to `unknown`, narrow once (const r = (raw && typeof raw === "object" ? raw : {}) as Record<string, unknown>), and pull the per-field coercions through the same String()/Number() style that src/lib/platforms/converters.ts already uses on foreign card JSON. The eslint-disable comments then go away with the `any`.
evidence: src/components/LoreBookEditor.tsx:50 `function parseSillyTavernLorebook(raw: any): LoreBook`, and line 70 `rawEntries.map((e: any) => ...)`.

Lines 51-58 annotate each extraction — `const scan_depth: number = raw.scan_depth ?? 50`, `const recursive_scanning: boolean = raw.recursive_scanning ?? false` — but because raw is `any`, a card storing "50" or "true" passes straight through under a number/boolean annotation.

The entry mapper is looser still: keys and secondary_keys get Array.isArray guards, but content, insertion_order and priority are taken with a bare `??`, so a numeric content lands in a field typed string.

issues.summary: Inbound bridge RPC params are cast, not checked, and callApp<T> lets each caller name any result type
issues.suggestion: In protocol.ts add one mapped type — interface BridgeCalls { "cards.get": { params: GetParams; result: GetResult }; ... } — and type callApp as callApp<M extends BridgeMethod>(method: M, params: BridgeCalls[M]["params"]): Promise<BridgeCalls[M]["result"]>. That removes the explicit <T> from every MCP call site. On the app side, guard the two fields that matter (typeof p?.id === "string", type against ALLOWED_CARD_TYPES) before dispatch rather than asserting.
evidence: src/lib/bridge/client.ts:260-271 dispatches with `req.params as ListParams`, `as GetParams`, `as CreateParams`, `as UpdateParams`, `as DeleteParams`, `as OpenParams` — the protocol declares params as `unknown` (protocol.ts:117) precisely because it arrives over a socket.
Only createCard validates anything (ALLOWED_CARD_TYPES at line 351); getCard/updateCard/removeCard/openCard trust params.id to be a string, and listCards trusts params.type to be a CardType.

On the other side, mcp/src/bridge.ts:230 `callApp<T = unknown>(method: BridgeMethod, params?: unknown)` ties neither params nor result to the method, so callApp<GetResult>("cards.get", {}) type-checks.
The protocol module already names a params and a result interface for every method, so the information needed to check this exists and is simply not connected.

add.header: Acyclic one-way layering across all 69 modules
add.description: A full import-graph walk finds zero cycles and no upward imports: types is imported by lib, lib by hooks and components, components only by App.tsx. A developer can predict where a dependency may point without checking.

add.header: Highest fan-in module is pure type declarations
add.description: src/types/index.ts has 29 importers but contains only interfaces and unions, so the coupling carries no runtime blast radius. The next hubs (platforms, pngMetadata) are self-contained data tables and codecs whose only imports are type-only.

add.header: Singletons are lazy, never import-time
add.description: Every module-scope mutable binding (IndexedDB handle, WebLLM engine, bridge socket, CRC table) is initialised on first use, and nothing touches localStorage or opens a socket at module scope, so import order never matters and modules stay testable in isolation.

add.header: Shared singletons use one subscribe-plus-hook protocol
add.description: The MCP bridge and the WebLLM engine both expose getState/subscribe pairs consumed by a one-line useSyncExternalStore hook, so the two pieces of cross-component state behave identically instead of each inventing its own propagation scheme.

add.header: Bridge inverts its dependency via a host callback
add.description: src/lib/bridge/client.ts defines a BridgeHost interface that App.tsx registers, rather than importing component state, keeping the lib-to-components direction one-way even for a module that must drive the UI.

add.header: MCP package shares src/lib through a dependency-free protocol
add.description: mcp/ is a separate Node package that imports four browser-neutral app modules by relative path so validation and platform rules have one implementation; the seam is documented in README.md and in mcp/src/index.ts, and protocol.ts is explicitly kept import-free for both sides.

add.header: Card-type polymorphism modelled by parallel code paths
add.description: The four non-character card types have no owning module, so their save/export sequence is duplicated across four editors, four state triples in App.tsx, a switch in the bridge client, and a saveCard/saveAnyCard split in the library. Changing save semantics is a five-site edit.

add.header: Layer direction holds: lib and hooks never import components
add.description: src/lib and src/hooks contain no imports from src/components; the bridge instead inverts control via registerBridgeHost(BridgeHost), which App.tsx fills in. This keeps transport and domain logic reusable by the Node MCP server without dragging React along.

add.header: Each src/lib subdirectory opens with a why-comment
add.description: pngMetadata, personaParser, personaLlm, cardShape, carrierImage, download and minimalPng all begin with a header explaining the failure the module exists to prevent, not what it does. A new engineer can justify each module's existence from its first ten lines.

add.header: MCP server reuses app modules instead of copying rules
add.description: mcp/src/index.ts imports validators, platforms and personaParser from ../../src/lib so validation and compatibility answers cannot drift from the UI's; only storage tools proxy over the bridge, because the library is browser IndexedDB. The README describes this split accurately.

add.header: Two ownership models for the five card types
add.description: The character card is owned by App.tsx with export/save in CardPreviewPanel, while lorebook/script/scenario/persona editors are self-contained and remounted by key. The asymmetry is why the same lifecycle is written five times in four styles.

add.header: Card-type vocabulary is redeclared per boundary
add.description: The same five-member union appears as LibraryCardType, CardType, CardShape, DetectedType and NonCharType, and bridge/client.ts casts between them. Adding a card type is therefore a multi-file edit with no compiler help.

add.header: Registries are typed and single-owner where they exist
add.description: PLATFORMS (lib/platforms/index.ts) and NAV_SECTIONS (Sidebar.tsx) are single typed tables driving every consumer including the MCP tools, which is the pattern the card-type domain is missing.

add.header: Uniform component export and props convention
add.description: Every file in src/components/ is a default-exported function component with a local `interface <Name>Props`; no `type` aliases for props and no named component exports. The only deviations are contract-driven — ErrorBoundary must be a class, ResizableTextArea is a forwardRef — so a developer can predict any component's shape from any other.

add.header: Shared scaffold across the four non-character editors
add.description: LoreBookEditor, ScriptEditor, ScenarioEditor and PersonaEditor take the same initialCard/initialImageSrc/initialLibraryId props, hold the same status/saving/savedVersion state, and are remounted by App via a key bump. The repetition is deliberate uniformity, which makes any single editor that diverges immediately visible.

add.header: Semantic Tailwind tokens are the styling vocabulary
add.description: tailwind.config.js defines bg/text/status/border tokens with AA-contrast notes and instructs using them over raw palette classes; components follow this and reserve inline `style` for computed values like progress widths. ScriptEditor's CodeEditor is the one island that hardcodes hex.

add.header: Per-card-type protocol drift is the recurring outlier shape
add.description: Convention breaks here are behavioral, not cosmetic: helpers added after the character path existed (cardShape, useUnsavedWarning, library-id threading through the bridge) were adopted by some card types and not others. When touching any card-type code path, check all five branches rather than assuming the pattern generalizes.

add.header: Card-kind union declared under four names
add.description: LibraryCardType, CardShape, CardType and DetectedType are structurally identical five-member unions in four files, which is why bridge/client.ts is littered with `as CardType`. protocol.ts is intentionally dependency-free, which explains one of the copies but not the rest.

add.header: src/lib splits arbitrarily between flat files and single-file dirs
add.description: Six lib subdirectories contain only index.ts while seven comparably sized modules sit flat, and bridge/ has two files but no index. The split does not track size or file count, so where a new lib module belongs is a coin flip.

add.header: No silent console swallows anywhere in src
add.description: A grep for console.* across all production source returns one hit — ErrorBoundary's deliberate componentDidCatch log. Failures reach the user through status messages or thrown errors instead of disappearing into a console, which is why error behaviour here is traceable from the UI alone.

add.header: Every empty catch carries a written justification
add.description: Bodyless catches in LlmStatusLight, SmartImportPanel, personaLlm teardown and mcp/token all explain in a comment why swallowing is the correct behaviour there. A reader can tell an intentional best-effort path from an oversight without tracing callers.

add.header: One error-conversion point per protocol boundary
add.description: Bridge RPC handlers throw actionable messages and a single catch in ws.onmessage turns them into response.error; the MCP server rejects all pending calls on disconnect rather than letting them time out. Errors cross the socket in exactly one shape, so neither half needs defensive handling per method.

add.header: Decoder distinguishes absent from corrupt card data
add.description: decodeCharaFromPng returns a corruptKey alongside a null json so callers can tell 'this PNG has no card' from 'this PNG has a damaged card chunk'. Both ImportPNG and DecodePNG render different guidance for each, because the two cases call for opposite user responses.

add.header: return null in personaParser is a strategy probe, not failure
add.description: The dozen `return null` sites in personaParser mean 'this format does not match, try the next strategy'; parsePersonaText itself is total and always falls back to prose parsing. This is why the module reads as null-heavy without having a null-returning error convention.

add.header: React layer guards I/O per component, not by rule
add.description: Five card editors wrap the same IndexedDB and PNG calls in try/catch while Library.tsx and the two image drop paths leave identical calls bare. Coverage tracks which screens were revised rather than any shared boundary, so a developer cannot assume a component reports its failures.

add.header: localStorage reads guarded, writes bare
add.description: Every stored-settings read try/catches into defaults; every write calls setItem directly. The asymmetry means a browser that refuses writes (private mode, quota) leaves in-memory state and persisted state diverging with nothing shown.

add.header: Library functions named for the decision they make
add.description: lib/ exports read as statements of intent - decodeCharaFromPng, detectCardShape, shapeForKey, getCarrierPng, classifyChunk, budgetInput, proveToken - so call sites are legible without opening the definition. This is why the codebase tolerates large files like personaParser/index.ts without becoming hard to navigate.

add.header: Regular convertTo/convertFrom platform family
add.description: src/lib/platforms/converters.ts names all eight platform adapters convertTo<Platform>/convertFrom<Platform> behind convertCardTo/convertCardFrom dispatchers. The regularity means adding a platform has exactly one obvious naming answer, which is why no drift has crept in.

add.header: snake_case confined to wire-format fields
add.description: snake_case appears only in types that serialise to the Tavern Card v2 / SillyTavern lorebook formats (TavernCardV2Data, LoreEntry) and in shorthand-construction locals that build them. Keeping the external spelling means the mapping to disk is inspectable rather than translated, so this is a deliberate boundary, not casing drift.

add.header: "Sort" is the product's word for field assignment
add.description: sortPersonaAuto, SorterSettings, SortTarget, runSort and the user-facing "Quick Sort" button all use sort to mean "assign pasted text into card fields", never ordering. Used ~100 times across 6 files and surfaced in the UI, so it is established product vocabulary rather than a misnomer - do not flag it.

add.header: Handlers are handle<SpecificVerb>, never bare
add.description: All ~45 React callbacks qualify the verb (handleExportPng, handleSaveToLibrary, handleImportScenario) rather than stopping at handleClick or handleData, so the generic handle prefix still carries information at the call site.

add.header: MCP tool schemas restate card field names by hand
add.description: mcp/src/index.ts writes each tool's inputSchema field-by-field instead of deriving from src/types/index.ts, and the bridge persists whatever it receives verbatim. Nothing checks the two vocabularies agree, which is the structural reason create_script's `code` could diverge from ScriptCard.content unnoticed.

add.header: "Token" carries three meanings
add.description: Token means the bridge pairing secret (getBridgeToken, tokenPath), an LLM token (countTokens, TokenBudgetLevel), and a React refresh nonce (Library's refreshToken prop). The first two are unavoidable domain terms; new code should avoid adding a fourth sense.

add.header: Platform behaviour is a data table, not a class hierarchy
add.description: src/lib/platforms/index.ts holds all eight platforms as a PLATFORMS record of plain data (field support matrix, metadata key, template vars), and converters.ts pairs it with free functions behind two switch dispatchers. A developer adding a platform edits one table entry and two functions rather than subclassing anything, and the UI's compatibility view and the MCP compatibility tool read the same table.

add.header: One wire protocol module shared by app and MCP server
add.description: src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts is imported by both the browser client and the Node server, and mcp/src/index.ts reuses the app's validators, PLATFORMS and personaParser directly. Cross-process contracts and rules exist once, so the two halves cannot drift.

add.header: No barrels and only one generic in the whole codebase
add.description: There are zero `export * from` re-export modules, so every import names a real definition site, and the sole generic function (callApp<T> in mcp/src/bridge.ts) is instantiated at six concrete types. Indirection here is earned rather than habitual.

add.header: Custom hooks encapsulate behaviour, not just state
add.description: useTimedFlag and useStatusMessage exist because the hand-rolled copies leaked timers and cleared early; useEngineState and useBridgeState wrap useSyncExternalStore over module stores that two views must agree on. Each documents the bug that motivated it, so none reads as ceremony.

add.header: Per-card-type logic is copied across six files
add.description: Each of the five card types has its own editor, its own App state cluster and its own import branch, so adding or changing a type means the same edit in six places. The cost is under-abstraction rather than over-abstraction, and it is the dominant abstraction defect in this codebase.

add.header: LibraryCard is a hand-rolled tagged union
add.description: cardType plus optional cardData/rawData: unknown encodes the discriminated union in comments instead of in the type, so seventeen `as LoreBook`-style assertions across App, Library, ImportPNG, DecodePNG and bridge/client recover by hand what TypeScript could narrow automatically.

add.header: Seven runtime deps, every one actually imported
add.description: package.json keeps a deliberately minimal runtime surface and an import scan of all 68 source files finds a real consumer for each. Nothing has been added speculatively, so a developer can trust package.json as an accurate map of what the app uses.

add.header: Acyclic import graph across app and MCP server
add.description: A full traversal of relative imports in src/ and mcp/src/ finds no cycles, so module initialisation order is never load-bearing and files can be read in dependency order.

add.header: Heaviest dependency is dynamically imported
add.description: @mlc-ai/web-llm is reached only through `await import(...)` and a module worker, keeping two ~6 MB chunks out of the entry bundle so users who never enable the local LLM never pay for it.

add.header: MCP-shared app modules are provably dependency-free
add.description: The MCP server imports app source across a package boundary, but the reachable slice (types, validators, platforms, personaParser, bridge/protocol) pulls in zero npm packages, which is why esbuild's --packages=external bundling works and why the server needs only ws, zod and the MCP SDK. src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts states the constraint in its header comment.

add.header: No overlapping libraries for any single job
add.description: One icon set, one zip lib, one IndexedDB wrapper (with raw localStorage reserved for small settings), one fetch call site, and hand-rolled PNG chunk handling instead of a PNG dependency — there is never a question of which library to reach for.

add.header: Lock files clean, duplicates confined to build tooling
add.description: Both lockfileVersion-3 lock files resolve every declared dependency, and the only duplicated versions (glob-parent, picomatch, content-type) are transitive dev/build tooling, so there is no runtime version conflict to reason about.

add.header: Cross-package sharing is convention-enforced, not tooled
add.description: Nothing mechanically prevents a future npm import in src/lib/platforms or src/lib/validators, which would silently break the MCP bundle at runtime since esbuild marks unknown packages external and mcp/package.json does not list them. The safeguard today is a prose comment plus reviewer discipline.

add.header: Strategy chain with small named predicates in personaParser
add.description: parsePersonaText composes four independent strategies with `??` and delegates every judgement to a one-line named predicate (isSeparatorLine, isBulletLine, isDialogueLine, isNameLike). A reader can follow the control flow without holding regexes in their head, and each predicate carries a comment naming the input that forced it to exist.

add.header: Comments record the failure that shaped the code
add.description: Across pngMetadata, converters, personaLlm and the editors, the non-obvious lines carry a note explaining what previously broke — signed-int chunk lengths, a regex matching English parentheticals, unmemoized BPE encoding on every keystroke. This makes defensive-looking code read as necessary rather than as sprawl.

add.header: Per-card-type internals are copied, not parameterised
add.description: Script, Scenario, Persona and LoreBook editors each carry their own copy of the same state block and save/export helpers, and App.tsx, ImportPNG and Library each dispatch over the five card types by hand. Adding or fixing a card-type behaviour is a four-to-six-file edit, and the copies have begun to diverge (finally vs trailing setSaving).

add.header: State updates use functional setState patchers
add.description: update/updateBook/updateEntry/setProject all take the previous value as an argument rather than closing over current state, which keeps mutation explicit and bounded to one call site. The one place that breaks the pattern (LoreBookEditor.deleteEntry) is the one place with a selection bug.

add.header: Binary parsing loops declare their own bounds
add.description: readChunks caps chunk length and chunk count and comments that every iteration consumes at least 12 bytes, so termination is provable from the loop body alone. Edge-case handling in this layer is precise rather than blanket-defensive.

add.header: Almost no migration residue at function level
add.description: Only three lint suppressions exist across src and mcp/src, each adjacent to a comment explaining the intent, and there are no deprecated-but-called helpers or dual-path legacy branches. Repeated code here is copy-paste growth, not a half-finished migration.

add.header: Shared wire contract in src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts
add.description: One dependency-free file imported by both the browser app and the Node MCP server carries the frame types, method union, param/result shapes, close codes and protocol version, with the handshake written out as a sequence diagram. Both halves of the bridge change together instead of drifting, and the duplicated crypto helpers on each side are a deliberate consequence of keeping the file import-free.

add.header: One narrow call surface per bridge half
add.description: mcp/src/index.ts never touches a socket: every storage tool is a one-line callApp<T>(method, params), while bridge.ts owns timeouts, single-client promotion and failing in-flight calls on disconnect. On the app side client.ts registers a BridgeHost callback set from App.tsx rather than importing component state, so the lib layer never reaches upward.

add.header: All platform translation in converters.ts
add.description: Every to-platform and from-platform mapping sits in one file behind the convertCardTo/convertCardFrom dispatchers, so quirks like JanitorAI's {{bot}} and Backyard's aiName never leak into components and a new platform is one function plus one switch arm.

add.header: Card-type fan-out spelled out longhand at every seam
add.description: The five card types are wired as five parallel callback props in Library, ImportPNG and DecodePNG, and as four key/init state pairs with eight handlers in App. Adding a type means editing four modules, and it is why fixes landing on one entry path (shape-based routing, lorebook normalisation) have not reached the others.

add.header: Import normalisation sits in consumers, not at the boundary
add.description: parseSillyTavernLorebook lives inside LoreBookEditor and runs only on that editor's JSON drop; the PNG and MCP entry paths use `as LoreBook` casts instead. The translation exists but not where every caller crosses, so payload shapes the detector explicitly accepts can still reach the editor unnormalised.

add.header: Editors share the same save/export choreography
add.description: All four non-character editors perform the identical getCarrierPng -> encodeCharaToPng -> downloadPng and saveAnyCard sequence, differing only by metadata key and name fallback. The repetition is real but uniform, and each step goes through the same small lib functions, so the pattern is learnable once and applies everywhere.

add.header: Tests use an independent PNG reader to avoid shared-bug blindness
add.description: src/lib/pngMetadata/index.test.ts re-implements crc32 and a strict chunk walker rather than reusing the module under test, because a shared parser would let a writer bug hide behind a matching reader bug. It asserts full structural invariants (per-chunk CRC, IHDR first, exactly one IEND, cursor landing on the final byte), so the suite catches files that decode fine here but are rejected by SillyTavern.

add.header: Support table is verified against real export output
add.description: converters.test.ts asserts that every field PLATFORMS marks full/partial/renamed actually appears in the exported payload for all 8 platforms, normalising away JSON escaping and deliberate placeholder rewrites. This pins the UI's 'fields lost' count to reality, so the app cannot lie about what an export dropped.

add.header: Mock-free, deterministic, regression-anchored tests
add.description: No test in the repo uses vi.mock/vi.fn, fake timers, Date.now, Math.random or env reads, and there are zero snapshot assertions; each case asserts named behaviour and most carry a comment naming the real bug it pins. The suite therefore has no test-production coupling and no timing or ordering fragility, and runs in 33ms.

add.header: Node-only harness caps coverage at the lib boundary
add.description: vite.config.ts declares no vitest `test` block and the project has no jsdom or testing-library dependency, so the suite runs in Node and can only reach pure modules. This is why coverage stops cleanly at src/lib and why components, hooks, IndexedDB persistence and canvas paths are untestable rather than merely untested.

add.header: Coverage clusters around modules that once had bugs
add.description: The four tested modules — pngMetadata, converters, cardShape, personaParser — are exactly the ones with documented past regressions, and their tests read as regression suites. Modules with no bug history yet (detectPlatform, archive dedupe, bridge handshake) have none, so coverage tracks incident history rather than risk.

add.header: Bridge wire protocol is a single shared typed contract
add.description: src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts is imported by both the app and the MCP server and names every RPC's params and results as exported interfaces, plus enumerated close codes. Because neither side can define its own shape, app/server drift is structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.

add.header: Observable singleton pattern reproduced identically three times
add.description: getEngineState/subscribeEngineState, getBridgeState/subscribeBridgeState and getSorterSettings/subscribeSorterSettings share the same signature down to returning an unsubscribe closure. A developer who learns one module's state surface correctly predicts the other two.

add.header: MCP tools share reusable zod field shapes
add.description: mcp/src/index.ts hoists `tags` and `openAfter` into shared constants and wraps every result in one text() helper, so the agent-facing surface reads uniformly. The value of this shows in the two places it was not applied (create_lorebook, update_card), which are the only irregular tools.

add.header: Card persistence split by card type at the storage layer
add.description: src/lib/library/index.ts keeps character cards (cardData/pngData/platform) and everything else (rawData/name/tags) on separate save functions rather than one record shape. This is the root of the divergent signatures and of the persist() adapter inside the bridge client.

add.header: Sorter options bag is silently backend-conditional
add.description: SortOptions presents settings/target/onProgress/signal as one uniform surface, but signal is honoured only by the endpoint backend and onProgress only by WebLLM. The type gives no hint, so cancellation appears supported on the default path and is not.

add.header: Editor components share an uncontrolled initial-props shape
add.description: PersonaEditor, ScenarioEditor and ScriptEditor all take initialCard/initialImageSrc/initialLibraryId and own their state; CharacterEditor is deliberately controlled because App.tsx owns the character card. LoreBookEditor's initialBook is the sole naming outlier in the family.

add.header: Single auth boundary, implemented symmetrically once
add.description: The MCP bridge is the codebase's only authorization boundary, and both halves derive their frames and constants from src/lib/bridge/protocol.ts, so there is no second dialect of auth to keep in sync. A reviewer can audit the whole posture by reading three files.

add.header: Server proves the token first, deliberately
add.description: The handshake has the server HMAC the client's nonce before the app sends any proof, because loopback is a shared trust boundary and a port squatter would otherwise be handed the secret. The ordering is documented in both protocol.ts and bridge.ts rather than left as an accident of implementation.

add.header: No legacy or tokenless bridge path survives
add.description: BRIDGE_PROTOCOL_VERSION is 2 and both sides hard-close on mismatch; the pre-handshake v1 behaviour left no shim, and README.md explicitly retracts its earlier claim that the loopback bind alone was sufficient. Nothing stale invites a developer to follow the old model.

add.header: Remote-endpoint gate covers the second data-exfiltration seam
add.description: The sorter's OpenAI-compatible endpoint is guarded by isRemoteUrl plus a remoteAcknowledged flag and refuses 3xx with redirect:'manual', because the local-vs-remote check is lexical and a redirect would replay persona text off-machine unwarned. The same care shown at the bridge is applied here.

add.header: Authentication is binary; no authority scoping after pairing
add.description: Once paired, the peer has full read/write/delete over the library with no per-method gating, confirmation, or audit trail. This is a deliberate simplification for a single-user local tool, but it means the UI's irreversible-action confirmations are not an invariant of the system, only of the UI.

add.header: Peer input validated inconsistently across RPC handlers
add.description: createCard checks cardType and image source while updateCard merges any patch and every handler casts params with 'as', so whether the bridge is treated as a trust boundary depends on which method is called.

add.header: Handshake has no automated test
add.description: The four test files cover pure card logic only; the sole authorization mechanism has no coverage of origin rejection, bad-token close, or session displacement, so a regression in it would be silent.

add.header: Comments name the regression they prevent
add.description: Comments across src/lib and src/components explain WHY by citing the concrete bug that motivated the line — the signed-int32 PNG length overflow, the deliberately absent Enter handler on the delete dialog, the corrupt IDAT length in the fallback PNG. This is why files like minimalPng.ts and useEngineState.ts carry a high comment ratio without carrying any noise.

add.header: Logging is eleven purposeful lines, all on stderr
add.description: The entire codebase has 11 console.* calls: one crash report in ErrorBoundary and ten bridge/server lifecycle lines in mcp/src. The MCP ones use console.error deliberately because stdout is the transport, as bridge.ts:100 states. There is no entry/exit tracing or object dumping to filter out.

add.header: Defensive checks sit only at real boundaries
add.description: Guards appear where untrusted data enters — parsed PNG JSON, localStorage, FileReader, canvas, user URLs — and each carries a note explaining what breaks without it (validators/index.ts:45-47, personaLlm/settings.ts:75). Typed internal values are not re-checked, so a reader can trust the type annotations rather than working around paranoia.

add.header: Shared helpers extracted rather than re-derived
add.description: download.ts is the single download path and archive/index.ts explicitly notes it uses the shared helper instead of a local copy; useTimedFlag documents the faults its hand-rolled predecessors shared; mcp/src/index.ts factors a create() helper and reusable zod fragments across tool registrations. The instinct to consolidate is present and documented — which makes the surviving editor duplication look like an unfinished pass, not a convention.

add.header: Per-card-type code is replicated, not parameterised
add.description: Lorebook, script, scenario and persona each got their own editor by copying the previous one, so save/export/clear/filename logic exists in four verbatim copies and App.tsx carries four parallel Init/Key state pairs plus eight near-identical handlers. Adding a fifth type means copying again rather than registering one.

add.header: No deprecation markers or migration TODOs anywhere
add.description: Across all 63 source files there is not one @deprecated symbol or TODO/FIXME referencing migrate, legacy, or 'remove after'; the three 'legacy' hits are explanatory docstrings on deliberate data compat. Nothing accumulates as a promise to clean up later, so a developer never has to guess whether a symbol is on its way out.

add.header: Removals are completed and written down
add.description: The Tauri desktop shell was deleted wholesale with zero surviving reference in src/ or package.json, and the README records why. Migrations here end with the old path gone rather than left behind a flag.

add.header: Versioned surfaces cut over rather than dual-run
add.description: The bridge pins BRIDGE_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 2 and closes the socket on mismatch instead of keeping v1 frame handling, and the IndexedDB store carries a real numbered upgrade path with one documented read-time normalisation. Both avoid the dual-path confusion that stale compatibility branches create.

add.header: Import routing split across two policies
add.description: src/lib/cardShape.ts introduced payload-shape routing to fix silent data loss on mislabelled cards, but only ImportPNG adopted it; DecodePNG keeps a duplicated CHARACTER_KEYS and the old keyword-only dispatch. This is the one place where a developer cannot tell which of two live conventions to extend.

add.header: Single class component is React-mandated
add.description: The lone class in the component tree is ErrorBoundary, which React still requires to be a class. It is not residue of an unfinished functional-component migration, so the 1-vs-29 class/functional split should not be read as drift.

add.header: Card spec support is v2-only by design, with one leak
add.description: The TavernCardV2 type, the validator and every converter target the chara_card_v2 spec exclusively; only detectCardShape also answers to chara_card_v3, which makes that one line the odd layer out rather than the start of a tracked v3 migration.

add.header: Strictly acyclic layering with no reciprocal directory edges
add.description: Imports flow one way through src/ -> components -> hooks -> lib -> types, verified by grep: nothing under src/lib, src/hooks or src/types imports a component. A developer can change a lib module without worrying about a cycle pulling UI code back in.

add.header: src/lib partitioned into single-concern domain folders
add.description: Ten folders (archive, bridge, customTemplates, library, personaLlm, personaParser, platforms, pngMetadata, tokenizer, validators) each own one concern behind an index.ts, so the folder name alone predicts what lives inside and where new code of that kind goes.

add.header: Tests co-located beside the module under test
add.description: Every test file sits next to its subject (cardShape.test.ts, personaParser/index.test.ts, platforms/converters.test.ts, pngMetadata/index.test.ts) rather than in a mirrored tree, so a move never desynchronizes test and source.

add.header: components/ flat dir hides three distinct ownership tiers
add.description: The 29 files split cleanly by fan-in into App-mounted pages, single-parent feature children, and shared primitives, but the flat layout and inconsistent 'Panel' suffix give no signal of which tier a file is in — so blast radius has to be rediscovered by grep on every edit.

add.header: mcp/ is a second consumer of four src/lib modules
add.description: The MCP server package imports bridge/protocol, validators, platforms and personaParser through ../../src/lib with rootDir set to '..'. Those four are deliberately DOM-free while their siblings are browser-only, but the tree does not say so, and mcp/tsconfig.json's hand-listed include has already fallen out of sync with the actual imports.

add.header: src/lib root files are small shared leaves, not stragglers
add.description: The seven .ts files at src/lib root total 238 LOC and are cross-domain utilities (download 6 importers, carrierImage 5, tavernCard 3); their presence beside the domain folders is a deliberate shallow-leaf convention rather than an ungrouped backlog.

add.header: No module-scope I/O or environment reads anywhere
add.description: Every localStorage, IndexedDB and network access lives inside an exported function, and neither process.env nor import.meta.env appears in the tree — the one build-time value is injected by vite's define. Importing any module is therefore free of side effects, which is what makes the lib/ modules testable and reusable from Node without a DOM shim.

add.header: Module singletons exposed via getState/subscribe pairs
add.description: Bridge state, sorter engine state and sorter settings each live in module scope because two independent UI surfaces must agree on them, and each exposes a getState/subscribe pair rather than a bare mutable export. The bridge and engine stores are consumed through useSyncExternalStore hooks, so React never sees a torn read and no consumer needs to care which mounted first.

add.header: Heavy engine and DB init deferred behind lazy getters
add.description: The multi-gigabyte WebLLM runtime is reached only through `await import('@mlc-ai/web-llm')` inside getEngine/isModelCached, its worker is constructed at the same point, and IndexedDB opens behind `getDb()` on first use. Keeping these off the import graph is why a cold page load costs nothing until the user actually asks for the feature.

add.header: Shared lib modules deliberately isomorphic for the MCP server
add.description: validators, platforms, personaParser, protocol and types contain no browser globals at any scope, and protocol.ts states the invariant in its header. This is what lets mcp/src/index.ts import the app's own rule implementations directly instead of maintaining a second copy that drifts.

add.header: No import cycles across the source tree
add.description: A full resolve of every relative static and dynamic import across all 63 non-test source files finds zero cycles, so there is no circular initialisation being hidden behind a lazy or conditional import. Dynamic imports in this codebase exist purely for payload deferral, not to break a dependency knot.

add.header: Bridge client's init contract is conventional, not structural
add.description: registerBridgeHost() and initBridge() are separate exports whose required order is upheld only by adjacent statements in one App.tsx effect, and every host use site is optional-chained so violating that order no-ops silently instead of erroring. This is the single place in the codebase where import/boot ordering is load-bearing and undefended.

add.header: IndexedDB schema migration is versioned, not order-dependent
add.description: The library store's upgrade path is gated on `oldVersion` per version step and paired with read-time normalisation of pre-cardType records, so a client on any prior schema converges without the caller having to sequence anything.

add.header: Variance expressed as data tables in src/lib
add.description: personaParser drives label matching off LABEL_ALIASES/JSON_KEY_MAP, personaLlm derives schema and prompts from FIELD_DOCS/TARGET_FIELDS, and platforms/Library/DecodePNG use PLATFORMS/SECTION_META/NON_CHAR_META. Adding a field or platform is a table entry, not a new branch.

add.header: Strategy functions behind a one-line entry point
add.description: parsePersonaText tries parseJson ?? parseWpp ?? parseLabelled ?? parseProse, each returning null to decline. The dispatch reads in a single line and each strategy stays independently testable without any registry or plugin machinery.

add.header: No wrapper or injection ceremony anywhere
add.description: 134 function signatures with zero pass-through wrappers, single-implementation interfaces or dependency-injection seams; shared UI pieces and hooks each have several real callers. Indirection that exists is paying for itself.

add.header: Card editors duplicate one shell four times
add.description: PersonaEditor, ScenarioEditor, ScriptEditor and LoreBookEditor each restate the same state block, filename effect, save/export handlers and export aside, differing only by card type and kind literal. Save semantics therefore live in four places.

add.header: Card type fanned out as four parallel callbacks
add.description: App, ImportPNG, DecodePNG and Library each declare or consume onLoad/onEdit Lorebook/Script/Scenario/Persona with identical signatures and re-branch over the same five types. The type is data everywhere else in the codebase but a hand-written chain on this path.

add.header: Lorebook format rules live in the component
add.description: parseSillyTavernLorebook, buildExportData and DEFAULT_ENTRY sit in LoreBookEditor.tsx while converters, pngMetadata, personaParser and validators are lib modules the MCP server imports. That is why mcp/src/index.ts restates the lorebook entry defaults.

add.header: Bridge handlers are two-phase by protocol design
add.description: Both mcp/src/bridge.ts and src/lib/bridge/client.ts put handshake and RPC dispatch in one socket message handler with per-connection closure state. The nesting is inherent to the protocol, not a mixed responsibility — treat future complexity flags there as expected.

add.header: Nullable parser strategies discharged at one entry point
add.description: personaParser's four strategies each declare `ParsedPersona | null` honestly and are chained with `??` behind a single total entry point, so callers never have to reason about which strategy ran or whether null can escape.

add.header: JSDoc records the bug each contract now prevents
add.description: Comments across lib/ explain why a contract is shaped as it is by naming the failure it replaced (silent field loss in parseJson, the signed-int32 chunk-length walk in pngMetadata, the detached-anchor download). This makes the contracts self-enforcing under future edits rather than merely described.

add.header: Public getX surface is genuinely side-effect free
add.description: Every exported getX reads without mutating; the two memoizing getters (getDb, getEngine) are module-private and the expensive public alias is named preloadModel, so the getter naming convention can be trusted at call sites.

add.header: Very few type escape hatches in production code
add.description: A repo-wide grep for as any / ts-ignore / ts-expect-error / as never / as unknown as over src/ and mcp/src/ returns 7 hits. The small census means each cast is individually reviewable, and most mark a real contract gap rather than routine noise.

add.header: MCP tool schemas drift from the app's card types
add.description: Tool inputSchemas in mcp/src/index.ts are hand-written Zod shapes with no compile-time tie to ScriptCard/PersonaCard/LoreBook, so a renamed or missing field (code vs content, lorebook entry ids) is only discovered when the card is opened in the editor.

add.header: rawData is unknown, enforced by cast at every consumer
add.description: LibraryCard.rawData carries lorebook/script/scenario/persona bodies as `unknown`, and all four consumers assert the concrete type instead of validating. The normaliser that would do this properly exists in LoreBookEditor but is only wired to file import.

add.header: Bridge persist() rebuilds cards rather than patching them
add.description: The bridge's persist() constructs a fresh LibraryCard from the merged body, which is why fields it does not model (pngData, platform) are reset on every agent update despite update_card documenting a shallow merge.

add.header: Branch comments name the failure, not the code
add.description: Non-obvious branches carry a comment explaining the concrete bug they prevent — signed-int chunk lengths walking the PNG cursor backwards, a number-valued field throwing before the type check can report it, {{char}}: shredding an example-dialogue block. A reader can tell which guards are load-bearing and must not be simplified away.

add.header: Guard clauses and early returns throughout
add.description: Validators, parsers, import handlers and bridge frames all reject invalid input at the top and return, so the happy path is the last thing in the function and nesting stays shallow even in the 600-line parser.

add.header: Exhaustive switches over closed unions, no default
add.description: convertCardTo/convertCardFrom, the bridge method dispatch and the openCard type switch all enumerate a TypeScript union with no default arm, so adding a member surfaces as a compile error rather than a silent fallback. The switch_no_default detector hits on these are by design.

add.header: Timer hooks clear before re-arming and on unmount
add.description: useTimedFlag and useStatusMessage both hold the handle in a ref, clear it before setting a new one, and clear on unmount — the two faults their headers say the hand-rolled versions all shared.

add.header: Correctness guards not carried to sibling paths
add.description: The recurring defect shape is a fix applied where the bug was first seen and nowhere else: App.tsx guards the filename effect with fileNameTouched while four editors do not, and LoreBookEditor normalises lorebook entries while the three paths that feed it cast instead. Reviewing one such fix means checking every sibling with the same shape.

add.header: Doc comments assert unenforced invariants
add.description: Several claims live only in prose — a one-megabyte payload bound over a four-megabyte constant, a never-throws promise over two rejecting branches, a token-gated handshake whose HMAC has no domain separation. Treat these headers as intent, not as verified behaviour.

add.header: Strict mode enforced in both packages, tsc clean
add.description: Root and mcp tsconfigs both set strict:true, with the root adding noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch; tsc --noEmit passes with no errors. The compiler is a real gate here rather than advisory, which is why annotations elsewhere can generally be trusted.

add.header: No escape hatches: zero ts-ignore, three any
add.description: There are no @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error or @ts-nocheck comments anywhere, no non-null assertions in application code, and only three `any` occurrences — all in LoreBookEditor's SillyTavern parser, each carrying an eslint-disable and a comment explaining the shape variance. Type errors get fixed rather than silenced.

add.header: Untrusted input validated rather than asserted
add.description: Foreign platform JSON (converters.ts), LLM output (personaLlm coerceJson/toParsedPersona) and MCP tool arguments (zod schemas in mcp/src/index.ts) all enter as unknown or Record<string, unknown> and are coerced field-by-field with typeof/Array.isArray/String checks. The types these boundaries hand downstream are earned, not declared.

add.header: Card-type union redeclared across six modules
add.description: The same five values exist as LibraryCardType, CardShape, CardType, NonCharType and the MetadataKey superset, plus raw literal arrays in pngMetadata, bridge/client and the MCP zod enum. They stay in sync by hand, and bridge/client.ts crosses between them with five unchecked casts.

add.header: LibraryCard variant invariant lives in comments
add.description: cardType is a discriminant but cardData/rawData are plain optional fields with the rule written as a trailing comment, so roughly ten consumers in App.tsx, Library.tsx and bridge/client.ts re-assert the payload type by hand. This is the single biggest source of load-bearing casts in the codebase.

add.header: Card payload normalisers bypassed on some entry paths
add.description: parseSillyTavernLorebook normalises object-keyed entries and missing fields, but only the drag-a-JSON path calls it; PNG import and library-open assert the type instead. The LoreBook annotation is therefore backed by a real check on one of three routes, which makes it a runtime hazard rather than a cosmetic one.
